drills.q: A pipeline runs on schedule, throws no errors, and produces a plausible row count, but a downstream revenue dashboard has been wrong for three weeks. Which dimension groups would have caught this, and which wouldn't?
drills.a: Freshness and volume checks would likely pass (the job ran, row counts look normal) — this is a correctness failure, not an availability one. Schema and especially distribution checks (e.g. revenue shouldn't deviate more than N standard deviations from a 30-day baseline) are what would have caught a semantically wrong value hiding behind a normal-looking run.

drills.q: A producer team ships a breaking schema change to an event payload. The consumer's dbt test catches it three hours later, after two downstream dashboards already updated with bad data. What's the structural fix, not just 'run the check sooner'?
drills.a: Enforce a data contract in the PRODUCER's own CI/CD pipeline so the breaking change fails their build before it ships at all, rather than relying on a consumer-side check to catch it after the fact. Enforcing downstream only ever detects damage already done.

drills.q: You need to validate raw, just-landed data before it becomes any dbt model, with logic too expressive for plain SQL. Which of dbt tests, Great Expectations, or Soda fits, and why do the other two not?
drills.a: Great Expectations — it validates data at a point dbt tests structurally can't reach (dbt only tests things it has already built) and supports expressive Python-based checks. dbt tests only run at build time on already-built models; Soda is designed for scheduled continuous observability on production tables, not a pre-model raw-ingestion gate.

drills.q: Explain with a concrete cost comparison why fail-fast beats fail-quiet for a bad row.
drills.a: Caught at ingestion: one row quarantined, no further cleanup. Caught three joins and a materialized dashboard later: you must identify every downstream artifact the bad row touched, correct or invalidate each, and possibly explain to a stakeholder why an externally-reported number was wrong. The cost compounds with every hop the bad row travels before detection.

drills.q: A financial-close pipeline and a high-volume clickstream pipeline both have a similar row-level validation failure rate. Should both circuit-break? Justify the different treatment.
drills.a: No. The financial-close pipeline should circuit-break — partially-wrong data in a financial report is worse than a delayed but correct one. The clickstream pipeline should quarantine bad rows and continue — a small, expected bad-row rate is normal at that volume, and blocking the entire pipeline over it produces stale data for everyone, which is worse than isolating the bad rows.

drills.q: Your team pages on-call for every dbt test failure. After two months, on-call has muted the alert channel. Diagnose the failure mode and describe the fix.
drills.a: Alert fatigue: most failures were low-impact or already-understood, so paging on all of them trained on-call to mute the channel — meaning the one alert that represents a real incident now fires into silence. Fix: tier alerts by the downstream consumer's business impact (page only for real impact, digest the rest), and periodically prune checks that have never caught a real problem.

drills.q: A stakeholder reports a wrong revenue number. With only table-level lineage available, what does diagnosis look like, and how does column-level lineage change it?
drills.a: With table-level lineage alone, you know gold.revenue depends on some upstream tables but must manually read transformation code to find which specific columns matter — potentially hours for a company with hundreds of models. Column-level lineage answers directly which input columns (e.g. silver.unit_price, silver.quantity) feed the output column and via what transformation, letting you check those specific fields for recent changes in minutes.

drills.q: A quarantine table has been silently growing for months because bad rows are isolated but nothing alerts on quarantine volume. What incident class does this represent, and how do you prevent it?
drills.a: A second, silent data-quality incident hiding behind the first — quarantining without monitoring the quarantine table just relocates the blind spot. Prevent it by alerting on quarantine-table volume crossing a threshold and treating sustained growth as its own incident requiring root-cause investigation, not just ongoing isolation.

drills.q: A source system migration causes a dbt not_null test to start failing on a previously always-populated column. The source team says the nulls are an intentional, expected change. How do you triage this, and what's the actual root cause of the disagreement?
drills.a: Quantify the null rate to gauge urgency, check whether this was a known/communicated change, and decide circuit-break vs quarantine based on downstream propagation. The actual root cause is the absence of an enforced data contract — without one, 'intentional' from the producer and 'breaking' from the consumer are both true with no shared source of truth, which a contract enforced in the producer's CI would have surfaced before the migration shipped.

drills.q: A vendor feed is reliably 2 hours late once a month due to a known billing cycle, and your static freshness threshold pages on-call every time. What's wrong with the check design, and what's a better approach?
drills.a: A static threshold can't distinguish a known, cyclical, benign pattern from a genuinely broken feed, producing a predictable false-positive page every month. A better approach uses a trailing-window anomaly-detection check (e.g. Soda's native anomaly score) that learns the cyclical pattern, or explicitly encodes the known exception so the documented monthly pattern doesn't trigger a page.
